entries.sentence: A common yeast infection caused by Candida, a fungus that normally lives harmlessly on the body, which can affect the mouth, the genitals and the skin.
entries.note: NHS: caused by a fungus called candida that is normally harmless; CDC lists vaginal, mouth and skin types.

entries.sentence: Thrush is an infection caused by Candida, which lives on the skin and in places such as the mouth, throat and vagina, usually without causing symptoms.

entries.sentence: It can cause problems in the genital area of women and men, in the mouth, and on areas of skin such as the armpits and groin.

entries.sentence: The NHS suggests washing the genital area with water or an emollient instead of soap, drying thoroughly, wearing cotton underwear, and avoiding douching and tight clothing.

entries.sentence: Thrush is an infection caused by Candida, a fungus that is normally harmless.
The CDC says everyone has Candida on the skin and in places such as the mouth, throat and vagina, and that most of the time it causes no symptoms.
The CDC lists several types of candidiasis, including vaginal yeast infections, oral thrush and skin infections.
entries.note: CDC: types include vaginal yeast infections and thrush; also skin infections and invasive candidiasis.

entries.sentence: The NHS says thrush can affect the genital area in both men and women, and can also appear on other areas of skin such as the armpits, groin and between the fingers.
Oral thrush, also called mouth thrush, is described by the NHS as usually harmless and common in babies and in older people with dentures.
Oral thrush in adults is not contagious, according to the NHS.
Thrush is not classed as a sexually transmitted infection, but it can be triggered by sex or, less often, passed on during sex.
In women, the NHS lists a white discharge that is often odourless and may look like cottage cheese, with itching and irritation around the vagina and vulva.
Stinging during sex or when passing urine can also occur.
In men, symptoms can include irritation, burning and redness around the head of the penis and under the foreskin, a white discharge, an unpleasant smell, and difficulty pulling back the foreskin.
Sometimes thrush causes no symptoms at all.
In oral thrush, adults may have a red mouth with white patches, while babies may have a white coating on the tongue and may refuse feeds.
The CDC adds that infection of the mouth, throat or oesophagus can cause painful swallowing.
On the skin, MedlinePlus describes intense itching with rashes in skin folds, the genitals and under the breasts.
The CDC describes skin infection as an itching or burning rash with skin breakdown.
Thrush happens when Candida causes infection. In the vagina, normal bacteria usually keep its growth under control.
entries.note: NHS summary (second sentence). First sentence is a restatement of the NHS cause line.

entries.sentence: The NHS lists several things that raise the risk, including antibiotics, poorly controlled diabetes, a weakened immune system, hormone replacement therapy and pregnancy.
Irritated or damaged skin, and irritating products such as perfumed washes, are also mentioned.
The CDC says pregnancy and hormone changes raise the risk of vaginal candidiasis.
For oral thrush, the NHS names asthma inhalers, dentures, long courses of antibiotics and cancer treatment such as chemotherapy.
NHS inform also lists dry mouth, smoking and radiotherapy among the reasons oral thrush may develop.
The CDC says babies under one month old and people with HIV/AIDS have a higher risk of candidiasis in the mouth, throat or oesophagus.
A GP may be able to confirm thrush from the symptoms alone.
If the cause is unclear, or thrush keeps coming back, a swab may be taken from the discharge to check the cause and test for other infections.
For men, the NHS says a GP will want to confirm that it is thrush and rule out other infections.
UK sexual health guidance on repeated vulvovaginal thrush also expects symptomatic episodes to be confirmed by microscopy or culture.
Treatment is usually an antifungal medicine, given as a tablet, a pessary placed in the vagina, or a cream to ease irritation.
The NHS says thrush should clear up within 7 to 14 days of starting treatment, and that partners generally do not need treatment unless they have symptoms.
If thrush keeps coming back, treatment may be given for longer.
For oral thrush, a pharmacist can supply an antifungal mouth gel.
The NHS says thrush can occur in pregnancy because of body changes, especially in the third trimester, and that there is no evidence it can harm an unborn baby.
entries.note: NHS pregnancy page (as returned in summary).

entries.sentence: Pregnant women are advised to see a GP or midwife before using any treatment.
The NHS describes anti-thrush tablets as not suitable in pregnancy, when trying to conceive or while breastfeeding, with a cream or pessary used instead.
entries.note: NHS summaries: should not take anti-thrush tablets; treatment can be cream or pessary.

entries.sentence: A baby can also catch thrush during delivery.
About 1 in 7 babies develops oral thrush at some point, according to an NHS trust leaflet.
entries.note: Kingston and Richmond NHS trust leaflet.

entries.sentence: Creamy white patches on the tongue, gums, roof of the mouth or inside of the cheeks that do not wipe off easily point to thrush, whereas milk residue usually wipes away.
entries.note: Returned summary of NHS-affiliated baby pages.

entries.sentence: If a breastfeeding mother or her baby has thrush, both are treated at the same time because it can easily spread between them.
Breastfeeding can continue during treatment.
The NHS suggests washing the genital area with water or an emollient instead of soap, drying thoroughly, wearing cotton underwear, and avoiding douching and tight clothing.
For oral thrush, it lists good dental care, rinsing the mouth after using inhalers, not wearing dentures at night and not smoking.
A GP appointment, or a sexual health clinic, many of which offer a walk-in service, is the route the NHS suggests for a first episode, treatment that has not worked or thrush that keeps returning.
Pregnancy, breastfeeding and a weakened immune system are also reasons to get advice, and a pharmacist can advise on treatment.
For oral thrush, non-urgent GP advice is suggested if there is no improvement after a week of mouth gel, if swallowing is difficult or painful, or if a baby under 4 months has signs of thrush.
The CDC separately describes invasive candidiasis, which can involve the bloodstream, and says most people are not at risk of it.

entries.sentence: Also called: Candidiasis or yeast infection; oral thrush is also called mouth thrush

entries.sentence: Caused by: Candida, a fungus that is normally harmless
Where it can occur: Mouth, genital area (vagina, vulva, penis) and areas of skin such as the armpits and groin
Sexually transmitted?: Not classed as an STI, but can be triggered by sex or, less often, passed on during sex (NHS)
Usual treatment: Antifungal medicine: a tablet, pessary, cream or mouth gel
Usual time to clear: Within 7 to 14 days of starting treatment (NHS)
Usually diagnosed by: A GP, sometimes with a swab, or a sexual health clinic
